about: The HLA64 words the disassembler writes in its HLA64 view. 'hla64' marks a word of the language as it is (github.com/marketkernel/html-hlaa64, docs/language.md); 'new' marks a word added here to make disassembled code read better — it is not (yet) in the HLA64 translator. Anything with no word of its own stays a processor instruction, which HLA64 accepts as it is.

words.description: Copies a register or a constant into a register.
An operation with the destination as its first operand: +=, -=, *=, &=, |=, ^=, <<=, >>=, >>>=.
Arithmetic and bitwise operators. Precedence is Go's: * / % << >> >>> & bind tighter than + - | ^, which bind tighter than comparisons.
<< shifts left; >> is an arithmetic (sign-keeping) shift right; >>> is a logical shift right that fills with zeros.
Sign- or zero-extends the low 8, 16 or 32 bits of a register.

words.syntax: clz(x), rbit(x), rev(x), abs(x), min(a, b), max(a, b)
words.description: Built-in functions that map to one instruction each.
A load or store: square brackets are memory at the address inside them. Without a type the size is the register's (8 bytes for x, 4 for w).
A memory access of a given type: u8 u16 u32 u64 zero-extend, i8 i16 i32 sign-extend, f32 f64 are floating point.
words.x86Example:
eax = u8[rdi + rcx]
rdx = i32[rdi + rcx * 4]
u16[rax] = ecx

words.description: Reads or writes at the address, then moves the address on by one element.
Two registers loaded from or stored to neighbouring memory in one instruction. `!` writes the address back first; `++` after the base advances it by two elements afterwards.

words.syntax: push x29, x30 / pop x29, x30
words.description: Saves two registers on the stack (stp …, [sp, #-16]!) or restores them (ldp …, [sp], #16).
words.example:
push x29, x30
pop x29, x30

words.description: The address of data or a function. In an ARM64 listing it stands for an adrp + add pair, which builds a 64-bit address in two steps; in .NET it is the address of a variable, a field or an array element (a managed pointer), or of a method.
A string literal used as a value is its address, as in C.
A constant NSString used as a value is the address of its object, as @"…" is in Objective-C. The object (in __cfstring) holds the class, the flags, a pointer to the characters and the length.
A conditional branch. The disassembler joins a compare with the branch that tests its flags into one line.
words.wasmExample:
if l0 < 2 { goto L473 }
if l5 != l1 { goto L35f }
words.x86Example:
if r14d < 2 { goto L1000006fe }
if eax != 0 { goto L1000006fe }
words.jvmExample:
if i >= count { goto L25 }
if len(args) <= 0 { goto L25 }

words.description: An unconditional branch to a label in the same function.
A place a branch goes to. Labels are named after their address.

A call. On ARM64 the arguments are already in x0–x7 (d0–d7 for floating point) and the result comes back in x0 (d0); in WebAssembly they are written in the parentheses, in the order they are computed, and the call is a value when the function returns one.
Returns from the function. On ARM64 the result is whatever is in x0 (d0); in WebAssembly, .NET and Java it is written after the word.
A jump to the start of another function: it runs in place of this one and returns straight to this function's caller.

words.syntax: fn name() { … }, fn name(l0: i32) -> i32 { … }
words.description: A function. An ARM64 program does not say what its functions take, so the header has no parameters and arguments arrive in x0–x7. A WebAssembly function declares its parameters and results, and the header shows them; so does a .NET or Java method, its types as ildasm or Java writes them (this, argument 0 of an instance method, is not listed).
A choice without a branch. With the compare before it, csel and friends become one line.
A comparison used as a value is 1 when true and 0 when false.

words.syntax: d0 = d1 * d2, d0 = float(x0), x0 = int(d0), sqrt(d0), fabs(d0)
words.description: Floating-point arithmetic on d (double) and s (single) registers, and conversions to and from integers.
words.example:
d0 = d1 + d2
x8 = int(d0)
d1 = float(x9)

words.description: Any line that is not sugar is an instruction — of the processor, of WebAssembly, of .NET or of the JVM — written as the disassembler prints it. HLA64 takes it as it is.
words.example:
dmb ish
bfi x8, x9, #8, #8
local.get 0

words.syntax: a <u b, a <=u b, a >u b, a >=u b
words.description: Comparisons that treat both sides as unsigned (the hs, lo, hi, ls conditions). HLA64 compares unsigned only for variables declared `unsigned`; registers in a disassembly have no declarations.
Unsigned division (udiv) and unsigned remainder (urem); `/` and `%` work on signed numbers.
The upper 64 bits of the 128-bit product of two 64-bit numbers. Compilers use it to divide by a constant and to detect overflow.
Takes `width` bits starting at bit `lsb` and sign-extends them (sbfx). The unsigned form is written as a plain shift and mask: (x >>> lsb) & mask.
Rotates right (ror) or left (rotl) by n bits: what falls off one end comes back at the other.
Byte-reversal within 16- or 32-bit parts, count of leading sign bits, trailing zeros and set bits.
A 32 × 32 → 64-bit multiply, written with the extensions it implies.

Read-modify-write of memory as one indivisible step; the result is the old value. The last argument is the memory ordering: relaxed, acquire, release or acq_rel. Also atomic_clr (and-not), atomic_eor, atomic_or, atomic_smax/smin/umax/umin and atomic_swap. WebAssembly's atomics are sequentially consistent (seq_cst) and add atomic_sub, atomic_and and atomic_xor. On x86 every locked instruction is sequentially consistent: lock add, lock xadd and xchg with memory are seq_cst.
words.example:
x8 = atomic_add(u64[x8], x9, release)
atomic_or(u32[x0], w1, relaxed)
atomic_add(u32[0x770], l0, seq_cst)
words.wasmExample:
atomic_add(u32[0x770], l0, seq_cst)
l2 = atomic_swap(u32[l1], 0, seq_cst)
words.x86Example:
atomic_add(u64[&counter], r14, seq_cst)
eax = atomic_swap(u32[rdi], eax, seq_cst)

words.description: Compare and swap: if memory holds the expected value (the second argument), the new one (the third) is written. Either way the old value is returned. On x86 it is lock cmpxchg, which leaves the old value in rax (seq_cst).

words.syntax: x0 = load_acquire(u64[x1]), store_release(u64[x1], x0), atomic_load(u32[a]), atomic_store(u32[a], v)
words.description: A load that later accesses cannot overtake, or a store that earlier accesses cannot be delayed past. atomic_load and atomic_store are WebAssembly's sequentially consistent load and store.
words.example:
x8 = load_acquire(u64[x0])
store_release(u32[x9], wzr)
l0 = atomic_load(u32[0x770])

words.syntax: f64(s0), f32(d0), ufloat(x0), uint(d0), bitcast(x0), fmin(a, b), fmax(a, b)
words.description: Precision changes, unsigned conversions, a bit-for-bit copy between integer and floating-point registers, and floating-point minimum and maximum.
words.example:
d0 = f64(s1)
x8 = bitcast(d0)
d2 = fmax(d0, d1)

words.description: A name that is not an HLA64 identifier — a Rust, C++ or Swift path after demangling, a .NET name such as .ctor or <>c, a Java one such as <init> or lambda$main$0 — written between backticks.
A jump to an address computed at run time — usually a switch statement's jump table.
Stops the program: brk and udf. Rust and Swift put one after a call that never returns and where a check fails.
A local variable or parameter of a WebAssembly function (l and its index) or a global (g), when the module gives it no name; named ones go by their names. They are the registers of a stack machine.
An assignment that is also a value (local.tee): the local gets x, and the expression around it uses x too.
Computes a value and throws it away (drop). A call whose result is dropped is written simply as the call.
c ? a : b in which a, b and c are all computed first, in this order. Written so when one of them has an effect — a call, an assignment — that ?: would hide.

A call through a table of functions (call_indirect): how function pointers and virtual methods work. The comment gives the type the function must have; another type, or an empty slot, stops the program.

Conversions named after their result. i32(x) of an i64 keeps the low 32 bits, of a float drops the fraction and stops the program when the value does not fit; i64(x) and u64(x) widen an i32 as signed or unsigned, and u32(x), u64(x) truncate a float to an unsigned number; f32(x) and f64(x) convert a signed integer or the other float, f32u(x) and f64u(x) an unsigned integer; the _sat forms clamp instead of stopping.

words.syntax: ceil(x), floor(x), trunc(x), nearest(x), copysign(a, b)
words.description: Rounding to an integral value up, down, toward zero, or to the nearest (ties to even), and the magnitude of a with the sign of b.

A WebAssembly instruction that has no sugar of its own, written as a function of the values it takes; its immediates, if it has any, follow the name in angle brackets. It means exactly the instruction.
Runs the first branch when c is not zero and the second otherwise. WebAssembly's if, else and end read this way when the condition is in the line.

words.syntax: switch x { case 0, 2..=4 { goto L } default { goto L } }
words.description: Goes to the label of the first case x matches, or to the default. A br_table reads this way, cases that go to the same place together, as do the JVM's tableswitch and lookupswitch; CIL's switch has no default, and when no case matches the next line runs.
words.example: switch l0 { case 0, 1 { goto L38c0 } case 2 { goto L3924 } default { goto L39ec } }
words.cilExample: switch A_0 % 4 { case 0 { goto IL_0022 } case 1 { goto IL_002a } }
words.jvmExample: switch i32(sum % 4) { case 0 { goto L32 } case 1 { goto L37 } case 2 { goto L42 } default { goto L47 } }

words.description: A local variable of a .NET method (V and its number, as ildasm names them) or an argument, by its parameter's name (A and its number when it has none); this is argument 0 of an instance method — a reference, or in a struct's method the address of the struct. They are the registers of the stack machine.

Fields and methods of .NET types. obj.field is an instance field and Type::field a static one. Type::Method(…) calls exactly that method (call) — an instance method with its object as the first argument; obj.Method(…) calls the method of the object's own type, overrides included, and throws NullReferenceException when obj is null (callvirt). Types go by their own names, without namespace or generic arguments; the assembly view writes them in full.

words.syntax: new Type(a, b), new T[n], null
words.description: new Type(…) allocates an object and runs its constructor (newobj); new T[n] allocates an array of n elements (newarr); null is the null reference (ldnull).
words.example:
return new Decimal(value)
V_0 = new Int32[8]
words.cilExample:
return new Decimal(value)
V_0 = new Int32[8]

words.description: An element of an array, read, written or its address taken; len(a) is the number of elements. Like the instructions, each throws IndexOutOfRangeException outside the array and NullReferenceException on null.
words.example:
V_1 += V_0[V_2]
if V_2 < i32(len(V_0)) { goto IL_000b }
words.cilExample:
V_1 += V_0[V_2]
if V_2 < i32(len(V_0)) { goto IL_000b }

words.syntax: i8(x) … u64(x), nint(x), nuint(x), f32(x), f64(x), f64u(x)
words.description: Conversions named after their result, as CIL's conv instructions do them: to an integer type an integer keeps its low bits and a float loses its fraction, and a result narrower than 32 bits is widened back — signed for i8 and i16, unsigned for u8 and u16; f32(x) and f64(x) convert a signed integer or the other float, f64u(x) an unsigned integer. The checked forms (conv.ovf) are written as instructions.

A CIL instruction that has no sugar of its own, written as a function of the values it takes; a type or member it names follows in angle brackets. It means exactly the instruction: add.ovf(a, b) adds and throws OverflowException when the sum does not fit.
Computes a value and throws it away (pop). A call whose result is thrown away is written simply as the call.

A local variable of a Java method: by the name the class keeps for it (LocalVariableTable, or MethodParameters for a parameter) where that name means one slot in the whole method, else l and its slot. Parameters are the first locals, this is local 0 of an instance method, and a long or a double takes two slots. They are the registers of the stack machine.

Fields and methods of Java classes. obj.field is a field of an object and Class::field a static one. Class::method(…) calls exactly that method: a static one (invokestatic), or with invokespecial a constructor or a super method, its object the first argument; obj.method(…) calls the method of the object's own class, overrides included (invokevirtual, invokeinterface), and throws NullPointerException when obj is null. Classes go by their simple names; the listing writes them in full.

words.syntax: new Class(a, b), new int[n], new int[n] { a, b }, null
words.description: new Class(…) makes an object and runs its constructor — new, dup and invokespecial <init> in one. new T[n] makes an array of n zeros or nulls (newarray, anewarray), new T[a][b] one with its sub-arrays (multianewarray), and new T[n] { a, b, … } an array with its first elements stored, as javac writes an initializer. null is the null reference.
words.example:
values = new int[8] { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 }
p = new Point(3, 4)
words.jvmExample:
values = new int[8] { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 }
p = new Point(3, 4)

words.description: An element of an array, read or written, and len(a), its length. Like the instructions, each throws NullPointerException on null and ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException outside the array.
words.example:
total += i64(values[i])
if i >= len(data) { goto L28 }
words.jvmExample:
total += i64(values[i])
if i >= len(data) { goto L28 }

words.description: Conversions named after their result, as Java's casts do them: i64 widens an int with its sign and i32 keeps a long's low 32 bits; from a float or a double an integer conversion drops the fraction, gives 0 for a NaN and the nearest limit for what does not fit; i8, u16 and i16 are (byte), (char) and (short) — the low bits, widened back to an int.

words.syntax: checkcast<String>(x), instanceof<String>(x), athrow(e), dcmpg(a, b), ldc<String>()
words.description: A JVM instruction that has no sugar of its own, written as a function of the values it takes; a class it names follows in angle brackets. It means exactly the instruction: a comparison of floats stays dcmpg(a, b) >= 0 where a NaN would make a >= b mean something else.
words.example:
if dcmpg(value, 1.5) >= 0 { goto L12 }
best = checkcast<Comparable>(items.get(0))
words.jvmExample:
if dcmpg(value, 1.5) >= 0 { goto L12 }
best = checkcast<Comparable>(items.get(0))

words.description: Computes a value and throws it away (pop, and pop2 for a long or a double). A call whose result is thrown away is written simply as the call.

String concatenation as javac compiles + on strings since Java 9: an invokedynamic call site of StringConcatFactory, whose recipe holds the constant text. concat(…) is the string of its arguments one after another, each as String.valueOf writes it.
words.example: System::out.println(concat("Hello, world! sum=", sum, " kind=", Hello::kindOf(sum)))
words.jvmExample: System::out.println(concat("Hello, world! sum=", sum, " kind=", Hello::kindOf(sum)))

words.description: A lambda or a method reference as javac compiles them: an invokedynamic call site of LambdaMetafactory. It makes an object of the functional interface whose method calls Class::method with the captured values first and the interface method's arguments after them.
